questions.stem: Which halogen can displace iodine from potassium iodide solution?

options.text: Chlorine, because it sits above iodine and is more reactive
options.explanation: The higher, more reactive halogen displaces the lower one from its halide solution.

options.text: Bromine only, because iodine cannot be displaced
options.explanation: Bromine also displaces iodine; any halogen above iodine succeeds.

options.text: Iodine, because like displaces like
options.explanation: A halogen cannot displace its own kind - no electron transfer occurs.

options.text: Fluorine cannot, because it is too reactive
options.explanation: Fluorine sits above iodine and would displace it; reactivity helps, not blocks.

questions.stem: In Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2 the bromide ions are

options.text: Precipitated out of solution as a solid
options.explanation: Bromine stays dissolved; no precipitate forms here.

options.text: Oxidised, rising from oxidation number -1 to 0
options.explanation: Each bromide loses an electron to chlorine, the defining change of oxidation.

options.text: Reduced, falling from 0 to -1
options.explanation: That is the chlorine change, not the bromide change.

options.text: Spectators, because their oxidation number never changes
options.explanation: Bromide's oxidation number changes from -1 to 0, so it reacts.

questions.stem: Why are sodium ions absent from the ionic equation?

options.text: They react to form sodium gas
options.explanation: No such product exists in these displacement reactions.

options.text: They are too large to take part in solution reactions
options.explanation: Size is irrelevant; the reason is their unchanged oxidation state.

options.text: They are spectator ions whose oxidation numbers stay +1 throughout
options.explanation: Unchanged species are stripped from the ionic equation to show the actual electron transfer.

options.text: They evaporate with the chlorine water
options.explanation: Sodium ions remain dissolved; they are simply not part of the redox change.

questions.stem: Adding bromine water to potassium chloride solution will produce

options.text: Chlorine gas, because bromine displaces chlorine
options.explanation: Displacement only runs downhill the reactivity ladder.

options.text: Bromide ions, because chloride donates electrons
options.explanation: Chloride would have to be oxidised, which bromine cannot achieve.

options.text: A brown solution of iodine
options.explanation: Iodine is not involved in this mixture at all.

options.text: No displacement, because bromine is below chlorine in the group
options.explanation: The lower halogen cannot oxidise the chloride ion of a higher halogen.

questions.stem: Which ionic equation represents bromine displacing iodine?

options.explanation: Bromine molecules take one electron from each iodide, giving bromide ions and iodine molecules.

options.text: Br2 + I- -> Br- + I2
options.explanation: The equation is not balanced in charge or atoms: two iodides are needed per bromine molecule.
That is iodine displacing bromide, the reverse of the asked reaction.

options.text: Br2 + 2KI -> 2KBr + I2
options.explanation: That is the full equation; the ionic form removes the potassium spectators.

questions.stem: State the rule linking halogen reactivity to displacement.
questions.modelAnswer: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of that halogen's halide ions.

questions.stem: Write the ionic equation for chlorine displacing bromine from bromide ions.
questions.modelAnswer: Cl2 (aq) + 2Br- (aq) -> 2Cl- (aq) + Br2 (aq), with sodium or potassium spectators removed.

questions.stem: Explain why displacement reactions of the halogens are redox reactions.
questions.modelAnswer: The displacing halogen's oxidation number falls from 0 to -1 as it gains electrons, while the displaced halide's rises from -1 to 0 as it loses them, so both reduction and oxidation occur together.

questions.stem: A mixture gives a brown colour when chlorine water is added, then turns purple in an organic layer. Identify the halide present and justify your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Iodide is present: chlorine oxidises iodide to iodine, which colours the aqueous layer brown and concentrates as a purple solution in the added organic solvent, matching the known iodine observations.

questions.stem: What colour appears when chlorine solution reacts with potassium bromide solution?

options.text: Pale green, as chlorine accumulates
options.explanation: The chlorine is consumed into chloride ions, not accumulated.

options.text: Yellow-orange, as bromine is formed
options.explanation: The liberated bromine colours the mixture yellow-orange.

options.text: Purple, as iodine is formed
options.explanation: Iodine is not a product here; bromine is.

options.text: White precipitate, as bromide precipitates
options.explanation: No precipitate forms; the halogens stay dissolved.

questions.stem: Adding an organic solvent such as cyclohexane helps because

options.text: It neutralises the leftover halide ions
options.explanation: Cyclohexane is not a reagent for the ions; it is an extraction aid.

options.text: It prevents the halogen from evaporating
options.explanation: Volatility is unaffected; visibility is the gain.

options.text: Halogens are more soluble in the organic layer, concentrating the colour there
options.explanation: The halogen product partitions into the organic phase, sharpening the observation.

options.text: It converts the halogen into a more reactive form
options.explanation: The solvent does not change the chemistry, only where the product collects.

questions.stem: Bromine added to potassium iodide solution gives which pair of observations?

options.text: Yellow-orange solution, colourless organic layer
options.explanation: Those are bromine's colours, not iodine's.

options.text: White precipitate, then dissolving in ammonia
options.explanation: Precipitates belong to silver halide tests, not displacement colours.

options.text: No visible change, because bromine cannot displace iodine
options.explanation: Bromine sits above iodine and does displace it.

options.text: Brown solution in water, purple organic layer with cyclohexane
options.explanation: Iodine forms brown in water and partitions purple into the organic solvent.

questions.stem: In the bromine-iodide displacement, the electron ledger shows

options.text: Each iodide loses one electron while each bromine atom gains one, two electrons in total moving
options.explanation: 2I- -> I2 loses two electrons; Br2 + 2e- -> 2Br- gains the same two.

options.text: Four electrons moving, two per iodide ion
options.explanation: Each iodide loses exactly one electron to reach iodine's oxidation number 0.

options.text: No electron transfer, as this is not a redox process
options.explanation: The oxidation numbers of both halogens change, so transfer occurs.

options.text: Electrons moving from bromine to iodide
options.explanation: The flow runs from iodide to bromine, downhill the reactivity ladder.

questions.stem: Which halide ion could NOT be identified by a colour change on adding chlorine water?

options.text: Fluoride, which would be oxidised to pale fluorine
options.explanation: Fluorine is above chlorine; it cannot be displaced by it at all.

options.text: Chloride, because chlorine cannot displace its own kind from solution
options.explanation: Chlorine is already the displacing reagent; chloride gives no colour change with it.

options.text: Bromide, which turns yellow-orange
options.explanation: Bromide does give a colour change and so is identifiable.

options.text: Iodide, which turns brown then purple
options.explanation: Iodide is identifiable by the iodine colours.

questions.stem: State the colour of iodine in an organic solvent layer after displacement.
questions.modelAnswer: Purple, once the iodine partitions into the added organic solvent such as cyclohexane.

questions.stem: State the colour changes when bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution.
questions.modelAnswer: The aqueous mixture turns brown as iodine forms, and the layer becomes purple if an organic solvent is added.

questions.stem: Explain why the same halogen can show different colours in water and in an organic solvent.
questions.modelAnswer: The halogen product partitions preferentially into the organic layer, where it is more soluble and more concentrated, and its visible colour there differs from the dilute aqueous shade.

questions.stem: Two unknown halide solutions both turn brown with chlorine water. Adding cyclohexane separates them: one layer goes purple, the other stays yellow-orange. Identify each.
questions.modelAnswer: The purple layer marks iodide, oxidised to iodine that collects purple in the organic phase; the yellow-orange layer marks bromide, whose bromine product keeps its yellow-orange shade in the organic layer.
